title: Der Riese und der Schneider
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 183. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng, Thurm, Rath). Opens with a few lines of jaunty inset verse as the tailor sets out.
about: A boastful tailor who never pays his bills talks his way into a giant’s service, then has to survive a string of ordeals the giant designs to be rid of him, relying on nerve and a tailor’s trade-tricks rather than strength. A few lines of jaunty verse open the tale as he sets out, and it ends on a genuinely open note — the narrator admits he is not sure the tailor ever came back down. It is one of the more comic entries in this stretch of the collection.

sentences.t: Einem Schneider, der ein großer Prahler war, aber ein schlechter Zahler, kam es in den Sinn ein wenig auszugehen und sich in dem Wald umzuschauen.
sentences.l: To a tailor who was a great boaster but a poor payer, it came into his mind to go out a little and look about himself in the forest.
sentences.i: It came into the head of a tailor — a great boaster but a poor payer — to go out a little and look about him in the forest.
sentences.n: Einem Schneider is dative: the thought comes to him (es kam ihm in den Sinn, it occurred to him). Prahler and Zahler rhyme in the German, and the pair sets the man up in five words.

sentences.t: Sobald er nur konnte, verließ er seine Werkstatt,
sentences.l: As soon as he only could, he left his workshop,
sentences.i: As soon as ever he could, he left his workshop,
sentences.n: The sentence does not end here — the comma runs it straight on into the rhyme that follows. nur strengthens sobald: as soon as ever.

sentences.t:
wanderte seinen Weg
über Brücke und Steg,
bald da, bald dort,
immer fort und fort.
sentences.l:
wandered his way
over bridge and footbridge,
now here, now there,
always on and on.
sentences.i:
he wandered his way
over bridge and plank,
now here, now there,
on and on without ceasing.
sentences.n: The German rhymes Weg with Steg and dort with fort; Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not rhyme, so the pairs are named here instead. der Steg is a plank bridge over a stream. The verse carries on the sentence begun in the prose: verließ er seine Werkstatt, wanderte seinen Weg …

sentences.t: Als er nun draußen war, erblickte er in der blauen Ferne einen steilen Berg und dahinter einen himmelhohen Thurm, der aus einem wilden und finstern Wald hervorragte.
sentences.l: When he was now outside, he caught sight in the blue distance of a steep mountain and behind it a sky-high tower which jutted up out of a wild and dark forest.
sentences.i: When he was out in the open he saw, in the blue distance, a steep mountain, and behind it a tower as high as heaven rising out of a wild dark forest.
sentences.n: hervorragen — to jut out, tower up (separable hervor-). Thurm is the 1857 spelling of Turm.

sentences.t: „Potz Blitz!“ rief der Schneider, „was ist das?“
sentences.l: “Potz Blitz!” cried the tailor, “what is that?”
sentences.i: “Good gracious!” cried the tailor. “What is that?”
sentences.n: Potz Blitz is a softened oath: potz avoids naming God, and Blitz is the lightning — roughly “good gracious”.

sentences.t: und weil ihn die Neugierde gewaltig stach, so gieng er frisch darauf los.
sentences.l: and because curiosity pricked him mightily, he went briskly straight at it.
sentences.i: and because curiosity pricked him hard, he went straight for it.
sentences.n: stechen here is to prick, to goad; the shared entry for stach was written for cutting plants. darauf los gehen — to make straight for something.

sentences.t: Was sperrte er aber Maul und Augen auf, als er in die Nähe kam, denn der Thurm hatte Beine, sprang in einem Satz über den steilen Berg und stand als ein großmächtiger Riese vor dem Schneider.
sentences.l: But how he opened wide mouth and eyes when he came near, for the tower had legs, sprang in one bound over the steep mountain and stood before the tailor as a great mighty giant.
sentences.i: But how he gaped when he came near, for the tower had legs, cleared the steep mountain at a bound, and stood before the tailor as a huge giant.
sentences.n: aufsperren — to open wide, of mouth and eyes; the shared entry for sperrte was written for einsperren, to shut in. das Maul is an animal’s mouth, so it is coarse used of a man. Was … aber here is an exclamation, not a question. stand is here the past of stehen; the same spelling is the noun der Stand later in the tale.

sentences.t: „Was willst du hier, du winziges Fliegenbein,“ rief der mit einer Stimme, als wenns von allen Seiten donnerte.
sentences.l: “What do you want here, you tiny fly’s-leg,” cried he with a voice as if it thundered from all sides.
sentences.i: “What do you want here, you tiny fly’s leg?” he cried, in a voice as though it were thundering from every side.
sentences.n: der stands alone as a demonstrative pronoun: that one, he. wenns = wenn es, and als wenn takes the past subjunctive — as if it were thundering.

sentences.t: Der Schneider wisperte „ich will mich umschauen, ob ich mein Stückchen Brot in dem Wald verdienen kann.“
sentences.l: The tailor whispered “I want to look about, whether I can earn my little piece of bread in the forest.”
sentences.i: The tailor whispered, “I want to look about and see whether I can earn my bit of bread in the forest.”
sentences.n: sein Stückchen Brot verdienen — to earn one’s bit of bread, to make a living. His voice drops here, and rises again the moment he is safe.

sentences.t: „Wenns um die Zeit ist,“ sagte der Riese, „so kannst du ja bei mir im Dienst eintreten.“
sentences.l: “If it is a matter of that,” said the giant, “then you can indeed enter into service with me.”
sentences.i: “If that is how things stand,” said the giant, “then you may as well take service with me.”
sentences.n: Wenns um die Zeit ist is an old colloquial turn — word for word “if it is about the time”; the force is roughly “if that is how it stands”, and the exact sense cannot be settled with certainty. in Dienst eintreten — to enter service.

sentences.t: „Wenns sein muß, warum das nicht? was krieg ich aber für einen Lohn?“
sentences.l: “If it must be, why not that? but what sort of wages do I get?”
sentences.i: “If it must be, why not? But what wages do I get?”
sentences.n: krieg is the first person of kriegen, to get — the shared entry for krieg gives der Krieg, war. was für einen Lohn, ‘what sort of wages’, is split around the verb.

sentences.t: „Was du für einen Lohn kriegst?“ sagte der Riese, „das sollst du hören.
sentences.l: “What you get for wages?” said the giant, “that you shall hear.
sentences.i: “What wages you get?” said the giant. “That you shall hear.
sentences.n: The giant throws the question back as a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the end: kriegst.

sentences.t: Jährlich dreihundert und fünf und sechzig Tage, und wenns ein Schaltjahr ist, noch einen obendrein.
sentences.l: Yearly three hundred and sixty-five days, and if it is a leap year, one more on top of that.
sentences.i: Three hundred and sixty-five days a year, and if it is a leap year, one more into the bargain.
sentences.n: fünf und sechzig: German counts the unit before the ten, and 1857 prints the number in separate words. The joke is that the giant offers days, not money.

sentences.t: Ist dir das recht?“
sentences.l: Is that right for you?”
sentences.i: Does that suit you?”
sentences.n: ist dir das recht — the dative dir names the person the bargain has to suit.

sentences.t: „Meinetwegen,“ antwortete der Schneider und dachte in seinem Sinn „man muß sich strecken nach seiner Decke.
sentences.l: “For all I care,” answered the tailor, and thought in his own mind “one must stretch oneself according to one’s blanket.
sentences.i: “As you please,” answered the tailor, and thought to himself, “a man must stretch no further than his blanket reaches.
sentences.n: A proverb: sich nach seiner Decke strecken, to live within what one has. in seinem Sinn — inwardly, to himself.

sentences.t: Ich such mich bald wieder los zu machen.“
sentences.l: I seek soon to make myself loose again.”
sentences.i: I shall soon find a way to get free again.”
sentences.n: such is the first person of suchen with the -e dropped, as in speech; sich los machen — to get oneself free.

sentences.t: Darauf sprach der Riese zu ihm „geh, kleiner Halunke, und hol mir einen Krug Wasser.“
sentences.l: Thereupon the giant spoke to him “go, little rascal, and fetch me a jug of water.”
sentences.i: Then the giant said to him, “Go, little rascal, and fetch me a jug of water.”
sentences.n: geh and hol are imperatives with the old -e dropped. der Halunke is a scoundrel, said half in contempt and half in fun.

sentences.t: „Warum nicht lieber gleich den Brunnen mitsammt der Quelle?“ fragte der Prahlhans und gieng mit dem Krug zu dem Wasser.
sentences.l: “Why not rather the well at once, together with the spring?” asked the braggart, and went with the jug to the water.
sentences.i: “Why not the whole well at once, spring and all?” asked the braggart, and went off with the jug to the water.
sentences.n: lieber here is the adverb ‘rather, sooner’, not the adjective ‘dear’ that the shared entry gives. mitsammt (modern mitsamt) — together with. Prahlhans, ‘Boast-Jack’, is a nickname for a braggart.

sentences.t: „Was? den Brunnen mitsammt der Quelle?“ brummte der Riese, der ein bischen tölpisch und albern war, in den Bart hinein und fieng an sich zu fürchten, „der Kerl kann mehr als Äpfel braten: der hat einen Alraun im Leib.
sentences.l: “What? the well together with the spring?” growled the giant, who was a bit oafish and silly, into his beard and began to be afraid, “the fellow can do more than roast apples: he has a mandrake in his body.
sentences.i: “What? the well, spring and all?” growled the giant into his beard — he was a bit of an oaf, and simple with it — and began to be afraid. “That fellow can do more than roast apples: he has a mandrake in him.
sentences.n: mehr können als Äpfel braten — literally to be able to do more than roast apples, that is, to be no ordinary man. der Alraun is the mandrake root, held to give uncanny power to whoever carries it; einen Alraun im Leib haben is to be possessed of such power. bischen is the 1857 spelling of bisschen.

sentences.t: Sei auf deiner Hut, alter Hans, das ist kein Diener für dich.“
sentences.l: Be on your guard, old Hans, that is no servant for you.”
sentences.i: Be on your guard, old Hans; that is no servant for you.”
sentences.n: die Hut is the feminine noun ‘guard, keeping’ — auf der Hut sein, to be on one’s guard. It is not der Hut, a hat, which is what the shared entry gives. The giant addresses himself by name, alter Hans.

sentences.t: Als der Schneider das Wasser gebracht hatte, befahl ihm der Riese in dem Wald ein paar Scheite Holz zu hauen und heim zu tragen.
sentences.l: When the tailor had brought the water, the giant ordered him to hew a few billets of wood in the forest and carry them home.
sentences.i: When the tailor had brought the water, the giant ordered him to cut a few logs in the forest and carry them home.
sentences.n: befehlen takes a dative of the person commanded: befahl ihm. das Scheit is a split billet of firewood.

sentences.t: „Warum nicht lieber den ganzen Wald mit einem Streich,
sentences.l: “Why not rather the whole forest at one stroke,
sentences.i: “Why not the whole forest at a single stroke,
sentences.n: der Streich here is a stroke or blow — mit einem Streich, at one stroke; the shared entry gives the verb streichen, to spread. The sentence breaks off into the rhyme that follows.

sentences.t:
den ganzen Wald
mit jung und alt,
mit allem, was er hat,
knorzig und glatt?“
sentences.l:
the whole forest
with young and old,
with everything that it has,
gnarled and smooth?”
sentences.i:
the whole forest
with young and old,
with all that it holds,
knotty and smooth?”
sentences.n: The German rhymes Wald with alt and hat with glatt. knorzig, gnarled or knotty, is a rare word; paired with glatt, smooth, it simply means every kind of tree, rough and smooth alike. er refers back to der Wald, so English says ‘it’.

sentences.t: fragte das Schneiderlein, und gieng das Holz zu hauen.
sentences.l: asked the little tailor, and went to hew the wood.
sentences.i: asked the little tailor, and went off to cut the wood.
sentences.n: This block opens in mid-sentence: the tailor’s question began before the inset rhyme (‘Warum nicht lieber den ganzen Wald …’) and only reaches its verb fragte here. Schneiderlein is the diminutive, little tailor.

sentences.t: „Was?
sentences.l: “What?
sentences.n: The giant’s astonished Was? opens a speech that runs straight on into the rhyme he repeats back, so the quotation is left standing open.

sentences.t:
den ganzen Wald
mit jung und alt,
mit allem, was er hat,
knorzig und glatt?
sentences.l:
the whole forest
with young and old,
with everything that it has,
gnarled and smooth?
sentences.i:
the whole forest
with young and old,
with all that it holds,
knotty and smooth?
sentences.n: The giant gives the boast back word for word; the one difference is that his repetition carries no closing quotation mark, because his speech runs on into the prose that follows.

sentences.t: und den Brunnen mit sammt der Quelle?“
sentences.l: and the well together with the spring?”
sentences.n: This block, too, begins in mid-sentence: the giant is still quoting, and the verb brummte arrives only in the next unit. mit sammt is printed as two words here and as one word, mitsammt, earlier in the tale — the 1857 text is not consistent about it.

sentences.t: brummte der leichtgläubige Riese in den Bart und fürchtete sich noch mehr, „der Kerl kann mehr als Äpfel braten, der hat einen Alraun im Leib.
sentences.l: growled the credulous giant into his beard and was afraid still more, “the fellow can do more than roast apples, he has a mandrake in his body.
sentences.i: growled the credulous giant into his beard, and grew more frightened still. “That fellow can do more than roast apples, he has a mandrake in him.
sentences.n: The same growl as before, with two small changes: the giant is now called leichtgläubig, credulous, and the colon of the first telling has become a comma.

sentences.t: Sei auf deiner Hut, alter Hans, das ist kein Diener für dich.“
sentences.l: Be on your guard, old Hans, that is no servant for you.”
sentences.i: Be on your guard, old Hans; that is no servant for you.”
sentences.n: Word for word what he said the first time — die Hut, the guard, again, and not der Hut, a hat.

sentences.t: Wie der Schneider das Holz gebracht hatte, befahl ihm der Riese zwei oder drei wilde Schweine zum Abendessen zu schießen.
sentences.l: When the tailor had brought the wood, the giant ordered him to shoot two or three wild boars for supper.
sentences.i: When the tailor had brought the wood, the giant ordered him to shoot two or three wild boars for supper.
sentences.n: Wie is used here for als, ‘when’, as it often is in spoken German. wilde Schweine are wild boars; the shared entry for schweine describes a dative singular, but here the noun is plural.

sentences.t: „Warum nicht lieber gleich tausend auf einen Schuß und die alle hierher?“ fragte der hoffärtige Schneider.
sentences.l: “Why not rather a thousand at once at one shot, and them all here?” asked the haughty tailor.
sentences.i: “Why not a thousand at once at a single shot, and all of them here?” asked the haughty tailor.
sentences.n: die alle hierher has no verb — the boast is thrown out as a fragment. hoffärtig is an old word for haughty, high-flown.

sentences.t: „Was?“ rief der Hasenfuß von einem Riesen und war heftig erschrocken, „laß es nur für heute gut sein und lege dich schlafen.“
sentences.l: “What?” cried the hare’s-foot of a giant, and was violently frightened, “let it be good for today and lie down to sleep.”
sentences.i: “What?” cried the coward of a giant, badly frightened. “Let that do for today, and lie down to sleep.”
sentences.n: der Hasenfuß, ‘hare’s foot’, is a coward; der Hasenfuß von einem Riesen uses von where English says ‘of a’. laß es gut sein — let it be, leave it at that.

sentences.t: Der Riese fürchtete sich so gewaltig, daß er die ganze Nacht kein Auge zuthun konnte und hin und her dachte, wie ers anfangen sollte, um sich den verwünschten Hexenmeister von Diener je eher je lieber vom Hals zu schaffen.
sentences.l: The giant was so mightily afraid that he could not close an eye the whole night and thought this way and that how he should set about it, to get the accursed sorcerer of a servant off his neck the sooner the better.
sentences.i: The giant was so terribly afraid that he could not close an eye all night, and turned it over this way and that: how was he to set about getting this accursed wizard of a servant off his hands, the sooner the better?
sentences.n: kein Auge zuthun — not to close an eye. je eher je lieber — the sooner the better. sich etwas vom Hals schaffen is to get something off one’s neck, to be rid of it; the shared entry for schaffen gives the plainer sense ‘to provide, get done’.

sentences.t: Kommt Zeit, kommt Rath.
sentences.l: Comes time, comes counsel.
sentences.i: Time brings counsel.
sentences.n: A proverb, printed without any conjunction: when the time comes, the remedy comes with it. Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat.

sentences.t: Am andern Morgen giengen der Riese und der Schneider zu einem Sumpf, um den ringsherum eine Menge Weidenbäume standen.
sentences.l: The next morning the giant and the tailor went to a marsh, around which round about a quantity of willow trees stood.
sentences.i: Next morning the giant and the tailor went to a marsh with a great many willow trees standing round it.
sentences.n: um den … ringsherum: the preposition um and the adverb ringsherum are split across the relative clause, and both say ‘around’.

sentences.t: Da sprach der Riese „hör einmal, Schneider, setz dich auf eine von den Weidenruthen, ich möchte um mein Leben gern sehen, ob du im Stand bist sie herabzubiegen.“
sentences.l: Then the giant spoke “listen a moment, tailor, sit yourself on one of the willow switches; I should dearly like, for my life, to see whether you are in a state to bend it down.”
sentences.i: Then the giant said, “Listen a moment, tailor: sit down on one of these willow wands. I would give my life to see whether you can bend it down.”
sentences.n: im Stand sein — to be able, to be in a condition to; der Stand is the noun here, though the same spelling was the past of stehen earlier in the tale. um mein Leben gern — dearly, for my life. hör and setz are imperatives with the -e dropped.

sentences.t: Husch, saß das Schneiderlein oben, hielt den Athem ein und machte sich schwer, so schwer daß sich die Gerte niederbog.
sentences.l: Whisk — the little tailor sat up above, held his breath in and made himself heavy, so heavy that the switch bent down.
sentences.i: Whisk — the little tailor was up there, held his breath and made himself heavy, so heavy that the wand bent down.
sentences.n: Husch is the word for something done in a flash. den Athem einhalten — to hold one’s breath (Athem is the 1857 spelling of Atem); einhalten and niederbiegen are both separable.

sentences.t: Als er aber wieder Athem schöpfen mußte, da schnellte sie ihn, weil er zum Unglück kein Bügeleisen in die Tasche gesteckt hatte, zu großer Freude des Riesen, so weit in die Höhe, daß man ihn gar nicht mehr sehen konnte.
sentences.l: But when he had to draw breath again, then it flicked him — because unluckily he had put no flat-iron in his pocket — to the giant’s great delight so far up into the height that he could not be seen at all any more.
sentences.i: But when he had to draw breath again, the wand flicked him — for unluckily he had put no flat-iron in his pocket — so far up into the air, to the giant’s great delight, that he could not be seen at all.
sentences.n: Athem schöpfen — to draw breath. The flat-iron is the tailor’s own tool and would have weighed him down; zum Unglück, unluckily, is said as though it were an ordinary oversight.

sentences.t: Wenn er nicht wieder herunter gefallen ist, so wird er wohl noch oben in der Luft herum schweben.
sentences.l: If he has not fallen down again, then he is probably still hovering about up there in the air.
sentences.i: If he has not fallen down again, he is likely hovering about up there in the air still.
sentences.n: wohl — probably, I dare say. The tale ends with the teller shrugging: the tailor is simply gone, with no return and no reckoning.

glossary.hut: die Hut — guard, keeping (auf der Hut sein: to be on one’s guard), not der Hut, a hat
glossary.krieg: kriegen — (I) get, receive (1st sg., colloquial for bekommen), not der Krieg, war
glossary.lieber: lieber — rather, sooner (comparative adverb of gern)
glossary.schaffen: schaffen — to get, put (sich etwas vom Hals schaffen: to get something off one’s neck, be rid of it)
glossary.sperrte: aufsperren — opened wide (3rd sg. past; Maul und Augen aufsperren: to gape), not einsperren
glossary.stach: stechen — pricked, goaded (3rd sg. past; die Neugierde stach ihn: curiosity pricked him)
glossary.stand: stehen — stood (3rd sg. past); also der Stand — condition, state (im Stand sein: to be able to)
glossary.streich: der Streich — stroke, blow (mit einem Streich: at one stroke), not the verb streichen
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, road (not the adverb weg, away)
